headline: CFTC Renews Technology Panel for AI, Crypto and Cyber Advice
dek: The 40-to-45-member advisory committee will continue examining technology in derivatives markets; the agency estimates $83,581.88 in annual support costs and does not pay outside members.

sources.title: Renewal of the Innovation Advisory Committee

lead.creator: Dclemens1971
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary CFTC headquarters photograph CC BY 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission headquarters at Lafayette Center in Washington. The agency renewed its Innovation Advisory Committee on Aug. 12.
lead.alt: Modern office complex housing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission in Washington.

charts.caption: CFTC projects approximately 40 to 45 members and $83,581.88 in annual committee support costs.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 40 to 45 members and 83,581 dollars and 88 cents in annual support costs.

charts.caption: The renewed panel's remit includes AI, machine learning, blockchain, prediction markets and cybersecurity in derivatives markets.
charts.alt: Graphic lists five technology areas in the CFTC advisory committee remit.

paragraphs: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has renewed its Innovation Advisory Committee to continue advising the regulator on technology in derivatives and commodities markets.

The Aug. 12 renewal notice says the panel will examine artificial intelligence, machine learning, blockchain systems, prediction markets, cybersecurity and other market-structure changes. Renewal does not itself adopt a trading rule or endorse a technology.

CFTC expects approximately 40 to 45 members drawn from market participants, registrants, technology providers, infrastructure firms, self-regulatory organizations, public-interest groups and academia. The agency says that mix is intended to balance affected viewpoints and technical expertise.

The agency estimates annual operating support at $83,581.88, including one-half of a federal full-time-equivalent position. Outside committee members are not compensated, and CFTC says it does not cover their travel or lodging.

The panel can advise on how financial firms use new technology and on the commission's own investment in surveillance and enforcement systems. Its recommendations are advisory; commission votes and applicable rulemaking procedures still control agency action.

The renewal record points to earlier work as evidence of the panel's role. In fiscal 2024 it approved five recommendations concerning artificial intelligence and six concerning decentralized finance, according to CFTC.

The commission also identifies crypto assets and environmental-based products among markets presenting fast-changing or novel questions. Naming those areas does not predict a future rule or enforcement result.

The practical test will be whether the panel produces specific, public recommendations that the commission can evaluate. Membership, meetings and resulting advice remain separate from legally binding CFTC action.
facts: The panel is expected to have approximately 40 to 45 members.
Estimated annual support cost is $83,581.88.
The estimate includes 0.5 federal full-time-equivalent staff.
CFTC does not compensate outside committee members.
uncertainty: The notice does not commit CFTC to adopt any future recommendation.
Future membership, meeting agendas and regulatory outcomes remain subject to separate agency actions.
seoTitle: CFTC renews AI, crypto and cyber Innovation Advisory Committee
seoDescription: CFTC renewed its 40-to-45-member technology advisory panel, with an $83,581.88 annual cost estimate and a remit spanning AI, blockchain and cybersecurity.

headline: NASA Plans for 50,000 Annual Citizen-Science Responses
dek: The agency is seeking comment through Oct. 13 on renewing a framework for public data gathering, image and sound classification, transcription and problem-solving projects.

sources.title: Information Collection; Generic Clearance for NASA Citizen Science and Crowdsourcing Projects

lead.creator: National Park Service
lead.rightsBasis: The National Park Service released the official documentary citizen-science photograph as a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.caption: A citizen scientist samples in Rocky Mountain National Park in an NPS photograph. NASA's renewed clearance would cover multiple public data-gathering and classification methods.
lead.alt: Citizen scientist kneeling beside field equipment while sampling outdoors in a mountain landscape.

charts.caption: NASA estimates 50,000 annual responses averaging 10 minutes, for 8,333 total burden hours.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 50,000 annual responses, 10 minutes per response and 8,333 burden hours.

charts.caption: Covered projects may gather observations, classify images or sounds, transcribe records and use participants for structured problem-solving.
charts.alt: Graphic lists data gathering, classification, transcription and problem-solving methods.

paragraphs: NASA is seeking public comment on renewing the generic information-collection clearance it uses for citizen-science and crowdsourcing projects.
The framework supports multiple projects rather than creating one new study. Comments on the renewal are due Oct. 13 under docket NASA-2026-0397.

NASA estimates 50,000 annual responses, an average of 10 minutes per response and 8,333 total annual burden hours. Those are paperwork estimates across covered activities, not a forecast of unique volunteers or scientific discoveries.
Data-gathering projects can ask participants to observe natural phenomena, document environmental conditions, submit photographs or samples, or respond through structured forms and surveys.

Classification and problem-solving projects can include labeling images or sounds, highlighting text or imagery, transcribing handwritten records and completing structured computational tasks or games with a purpose.

A project can operate independently or place a citizen-science method inside a larger NASA activity. Each collection still must fit the approved framework and applicable privacy and information-management requirements.

NASA says public participation can combine ground observations with satellite data and expand scientific understanding. The notice does not claim that every volunteer submission will be accurate or used in a published result; project-specific validation remains essential.

The agency is asking whether the collection has practical utility, whether its burden estimate is accurate and how it can improve clarity or reduce participant burden. OMB review follows the comment period.
facts: Comments are due Oct. 13, 2026.
NASA estimates 50,000 annual responses.
Estimated average response time is 10 minutes.
Estimated annual burden is 8,333 hours.
uncertainty: The notice renews a generic framework and does not specify participation in each future project.
Scientific use and validation will depend on each project's design and submitted data.
seoTitle: NASA citizen science clearance estimates 50,000 annual responses
seoDescription: NASA seeks comment by Oct. 13 on citizen-science data gathering and classification, estimating 50,000 annual responses and 8,333 burden hours.

headline: FERC Opens Mountain Valley Pipeline Boost Review to Comment
dek: The proposal would add or upgrade four compressor sites for 600,000 dekatherms a day of service; comments on the environmental assessment are due Sept. 8.

sources.title: Mountain Valley Pipeline, LLC; Notice of Availability of the Environmental Assessment for the Proposed Mountain Valley Pipeline Boost Project

lead.creator: Jet Lowe / Historic American Engineering Record
lead.rightsBasis: The Library of Congress provides the Historic American Engineering Record documentary photograph as a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.attribution: Jet Lowe / HAER, Library of Congress, public domain
lead.caption: A documented natural-gas pumping station in Burnsville, West Virginia. The FERC review concerns separate existing and proposed Mountain Valley compressor facilities in West Virginia and Virginia.
lead.alt: Industrial natural-gas pumping station buildings and equipment in a West Virginia landscape.

charts.caption: Mountain Valley seeks about 600,000 dekatherms per day of incremental service through compressor additions and upgrades.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 600,000 dekatherms per day of proposed incremental pipeline service.

charts.caption: The proposal spans Bradshaw, Harris and Stallworth sites in West Virginia plus a new Swann compressor station in Virginia, totaling 265,750 added horsepower.
charts.alt: Graphic lists four compressor sites and 265,750 horsepower of proposed additions.

paragraphs: Federal energy regulators have released an environmental assessment for the Mountain Valley Pipeline Boost Project and are taking comments through 5 p.m. Eastern on Sept. 8.

Mountain Valley Pipeline LLC seeks authorization for about 600,000 dekatherms per day of incremental natural-gas service on its existing mainline. The environmental assessment is an analytical record, not approval to build or operate the project.
At the Bradshaw Compressor Station in Wetzel County, West Virginia, the proposal would add a 23,470-horsepower turbine and auxiliary facilities.

At the Harris station in Braxton County, it would add 52,500 horsepower and restage two existing turbines. At Stallworth in Fayette County, it would add two turbines and upgrade two others for 52,880 horsepower.

In Montgomery County, Virginia, the proposal includes a new Swann Compressor Station with three turbines totaling 136,900 horsepower, a 0.2-mile 42-inch dual-lay connection and related valves and equipment.
Those additions total 265,750 horsepower across the four sites. The figure describes proposed equipment capacity, not continuous fuel consumption, emissions or delivered gas volume.

FERC is the lead agency for the Natural Gas Act certificate review. It says the environmental assessment examines effects, alternatives and mitigation; the commission will separately weigh need, economics and environmental consequences before deciding whether the project serves the public convenience and necessity.

Comments can address the assessment without making the filer an intervenor. Only parties with intervenor status have the procedural rights to seek rehearing or judicial review, and the notice says the ordinary timely-intervention period has expired.
facts: Comments are due Sept. 8, 2026 at 5 p.m. Eastern.
Requested incremental service is about 600,000 dekatherms per day.
Proposed added compressor capacity totals 265,750 horsepower.
The facilities span three West Virginia sites and one new Virginia station.
uncertainty: FERC has not decided whether to authorize the project.
Final requirements and environmental mitigation can change after review of the record.
seoTitle: Mountain Valley Pipeline Boost environmental assessment opens for comment
seoDescription: FERC is taking comments through Sept. 8 on a four-site Mountain Valley compressor proposal for 600,000 dekatherms per day of added service.

headline: NOAA Seeks Comment on Right-Whale Vessel Speed Records
dek: The agency proposes no changes to required safety-deviation logs and voluntary operator surveys, estimating 3,624 respondents and 674 annual burden hours.

sources.title: Implementation of Vessel Speed Restrictions To Reduce the Threat of Ship Collisions With North Atlantic Right Whales

lead.creator: National Marine Sanctuaries / NOAA
lead.rightsBasis: NOAA's National Marine Sanctuaries released the official documentary right-whale photograph as a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.attribution: National Marine Sanctuaries / NOAA, public domain
lead.caption: A North Atlantic right whale photographed under NOAA research permit 775-1875. NOAA is seeking comment on renewing records connected to vessel-speed protections.
lead.alt: North Atlantic right whale surfacing in open ocean water.

charts.caption: NOAA estimates 3,624 respondents and 674 annual burden hours, with no public out-of-pocket cost.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 3,624 respondents, 674 burden hours and zero estimated public cost.

charts.caption: A safety-deviation log entry is required when the regulatory exception is used; operator surveys and focus groups are voluntary.
charts.alt: Graphic distinguishes required vessel log entries from voluntary surveys and focus groups.

paragraphs: NOAA is seeking comment on renewing the information collection connected to vessel-speed restrictions intended to reduce ship strikes involving North Atlantic right whales.
The agency proposes an extension without revision. Comments are due Oct. 13; the current approval expires Jan. 31, 2027.

A vessel operator using the safety exception to exceed a covered speed limit must make a logbook entry documenting why the deviation was needed for safe maneuverability. The paper records generally remain aboard the vessel unless federal authorities request them.

NOAA separately surveys pleasure-yacht and large ocean-going-vessel operators about time on the water, awareness of whales, knowledge of speed-reduction efforts and preferred outreach methods. Those electronic surveys and focus groups are voluntary.
The agency estimates 3,624 respondents and 674 total annual burden hours. It projects no direct annual cost to the public beyond the time required to respond.
Estimated response time ranges from five minutes for a safety-deviation log entry to one hour for an electronic survey and two and a half hours for a focus group.
This notice concerns records and outreach research. It does not amend the geographic scope, seasonal dates or speed limit in the underlying right-whale vessel-speed rule.

NOAA is asking whether the collection is useful, whether its estimates are sound and how it can reduce burden or improve clarity. Any later change to the actual speed regulation would require a separate legal process.
facts: Comments are due Oct. 13, 2026.
NOAA estimates 3,624 respondents and 674 annual burden hours.
Safety-exception logbook entries are required; surveys are voluntary.
The current information-collection approval expires Jan. 31, 2027.
uncertainty: OMB has not yet acted on the requested renewal.
The information-collection notice does not change the underlying vessel-speed regulation.
seoTitle: NOAA seeks comment on right-whale vessel speed records renewal
seoDescription: NOAA proposes renewing right-whale vessel-speed logs and surveys without revision, estimating 3,624 respondents and 674 annual burden hours.

headline: HHS Withdraws 2008 Foster-Care Data Proposal
dek: The unfinalized proposal covered state reporting on out-of-home care, adoption and guardianship and related penalty rules; its withdrawal takes effect Aug. 12.
entities: Department of Health and Human Services

sources.title: Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System
sources.publisher: Department of Health and Human Services

lead.creator: Carol M. Highsmith
lead.rightsBasis: Carol M. Highsmith dedicated the documentary HHS headquarters photograph to the public domain through the Library of Congress.
lead.attribution: Carol M. Highsmith / Library of Congress, public domain
lead.caption: The Hubert H. Humphrey Building, headquarters of the Department of Health and Human Services. HHS withdrew an unfinalized 2008 child-welfare data proposal.
lead.alt: Brutalist Hubert H. Humphrey federal office building near Capitol Hill in Washington.

charts.caption: HHS proposed the AFCARS changes Jan. 11, 2008, never finalized them and withdrew the proposal effective Aug. 12, 2026.
charts.alt: Graphic shows the 2008 proposal and its 2026 withdrawal.

charts.caption: The withdrawn proposal addressed state data on out-of-home care, subsidized adoption and guardianship, plus specified federal penalty provisions.
charts.alt: Graphic lists foster care, adoption, guardianship and penalty reporting topics.

paragraphs: The Department of Health and Human Services has withdrawn a foster-care and adoption data proposal that had remained unfinished since 2008.

The withdrawal took effect Aug. 12. It removes the dormant proposal from the rulemaking docket; it does not erase current Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System requirements already established through other final rules.

The January 2008 proposal would have revised the data states report to the Administration for Children and Families about children in out-of-home care and in subsidized adoption or guardianship arrangements.

It also contained provisions implementing AFCARS penalty requirements from the Adoption Promotion Act of 2003. Because the proposal was never finalized, those proposed provisions did not become operative through that docket.

HHS says nearly 20 years passed across multiple administrations without an effort to finalize the rule. The department describes withdrawal as a way to reduce public confusion about current priorities.
A withdrawal is procedurally different from repealing a final regulation. No binding requirement created by the 2008 proposal is being rescinded because the proposal never reached final-rule status.

States still have child-welfare data responsibilities under the statutes and final regulations now in force. Agencies and researchers should use the current Code of Federal Regulations and current ACF technical guidance rather than the withdrawn proposal.

HHS could address similar reporting subjects in a future proposal, but it would need a new record and the applicable notice-and-comment process. This withdrawal makes no commitment about such a future action.
facts: The proposal was originally published Jan. 11, 2008.
Withdrawal is effective Aug. 12, 2026.
The proposal concerned out-of-home care, adoption and guardianship data.
The proposal was never finalized.
uncertainty: HHS does not say whether it will propose related reporting changes later.
Current obligations depend on statutes and final regulations outside the withdrawn proposal.
seoTitle: HHS withdraws 2008 AFCARS foster care data proposal
seoDescription: HHS withdrew an unfinalized 2008 proposal on foster-care, adoption and guardianship reporting; current final AFCARS rules remain separate.

headline: U.S. Tops Oregon 2026 World U20 Table With 12 Golds
dek: The host team finished with 24 medals, ahead of Kenya's 11; Italy ranked third with three golds after five days of competition at Hayward Field.

sources.title: Taylor anchors USA to world U20 4x100m record in Oregon

lead.creator: Rick Obst
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary Hayward Field photograph CC BY 2.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: Hayward Field at the University of Oregon, site of the 2026 World Athletics U20 Championships.
lead.alt: Modern Hayward Field track-and-field stadium on the University of Oregon campus.

charts.caption: The United States led with 12 golds and 24 medals; Kenya had four golds and 11 medals; Italy ranked third with three golds and five medals.
charts.alt: Graphic compares the top three countries in the Oregon 2026 medal table.

charts.caption: World Athletics reported a 38.16 world U20 men's 4x100-meter record by the United States on the final day, subject to ratification.
charts.alt: Graphic shows the United States under-20 4x100-meter time of 38.16 seconds pending ratification.

paragraphs: The United States finished atop the medal table at the 2026 World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene with 12 gold medals and 24 medals overall.
World Athletics' final table lists the host team with 12 gold, seven silver and five bronze medals after competition at Hayward Field from Aug. 5 through Aug. 9.
Kenya ranked second with four golds, three silvers and four bronzes for 11 total medals. Italy placed third in the ranking with three golds and two bronzes, five medals overall.
Jamaica ranked fourth with two golds and eight total medals. Australia and Ethiopia each recorded two golds, three silvers and one bronze and shared the next medal rank.
The ranking orders teams primarily by gold medals, then silver and bronze, rather than by total medals alone. That is why Italy's five-medal total ranked above Jamaica's eight.

On the final day, the U.S. men's 4x100-meter team ran 38.16. World Athletics reported it as a world U20 record with an asterisk, indicating the performance remains subject to the governing body's ratification process.
The final table is distinct from the placing table, which awards points for deeper finishes. This article reports medal rank and does not treat the two systems as interchangeable.

The result closes a championship Boho News previously covered at its opening. The medal table was updated shortly after the final session and provides the governing body's authoritative event-level count.
facts: The United States won 12 golds and 24 total medals.
Kenya won four golds and 11 total medals.
Italy ranked third with three golds and five total medals.
Competition ran Aug. 5–9, 2026 at Hayward Field.
uncertainty: The reported 38.16 world U20 relay record remains subject to formal ratification.
World Athletics can correct results after protests, eligibility reviews or data audits.
seoTitle: Oregon 2026 World U20 medal table: U.S. leads with 12 golds
seoDescription: The United States topped the Oregon 2026 World U20 medal table with 12 golds and 24 medals, ahead of Kenya and third-ranked Italy.
